This page preserves the former SGB geometry-level surface-distance-band design for readers of older notes and results. The producer and its API have been withdrawn from current SCGSim; use the [current SGB concept](../concepts/geometry.qmd) for the retained source-to-CAD process. Palace native Mask/Inset is a separate solver setting, described in the [Palace contract](../specs/palace-electrostatic-sgb.qmd#native-multi-margin-surface-epr).

::: {.callout-warning title="Historical design; not a current usage recipe"}
The figures and observations below describe an earlier implementation. They do not establish that the current package can create these geometric bands or that a Palace executable accepts a native Mask/Inset setting. Check the current source contract and the exact Palace executable before preparing a new model.
:::

### Historical design: SGB surface-distance bands (withdrawn) {#distance-bands}

This section records an earlier design only. The current SCGSim source does not expose its geometry producer, so the API examples below are not current usage instructions. Native Palace Mask/Inset margins remain separate and require a Palace executable that supports them.

The user first selects an actual **parent surface** from the effective model's surface catalogue, then specifies its source ownership, cut distances and original edges that define the distance origin.
A parent is not a plane guessed from a metal name: the same object can have several surfaces, hole rings and walls.
Selecting all original edges includes both exterior and hole rings; an explicit subset uses only those selected original edges.

Here, the selected parent is the completed left support: the rectangle $[-2,3]\times[0,2]$ µm with its original hole, retaining its adjacency to the substrate and upper vacuum.
On this plane, $d$ is the planar distance to the selected original boundary. Cuts at 0.125 and 0.25 µm produce the three disjoint bands in @fig-sgb-bands.
These two distances are explicit requests for this example, not automatic defaults for every model.

::: {#fig-sgb-bands .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-planned-bands.html" title="Planned distance bands on the completed left parent surface" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Planned distance bands on the completed left parent surface
:::

The parent in @fig-sgb-bands is the completed rectangle minus its hole, with a total area of 9 µm².
Bands also form around the hole. Concave corners or holes can give a band more than one connected component, so the three bands produce six child surfaces here.
P1, P2, P5 and P6 remain as reference points on the exterior boundary.

::: {.askr-table-compact .askr-table-numeric}
| Band | Range | Child surfaces | Area (µm²) |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| C0 | $0\le d<0.125$ | 2 | 2.236324 |
| C1 | $0.125\le d<0.25$ | 1 | 2.209366 |
| C2 | $d\ge0.25$ | 3 | 4.554310 |
:::

To inspect “at least 0.125 µm from the boundary,” select C1 and C2; “at least 0.25 µm” selects C2 alone.
These cumulative selections overlap, so their separately calculated results cannot be added as though the regions were disjoint.
The partition retains the original hole and the small connected regions within each band.

::: {.callout-note title="Partition seams are not new distance origins"}
Distance origins come from the parent's original physical boundary.
Neither the internal seam removed by the metal/end union nor the new seams between distance bands become additional edges from which to inset again.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Pass the selection request to the source plan"}
Use `surface_distance_band_catalogue(...)` to read actual parents from the corresponding construction plan, create a `SurfaceDistanceBandSpec`, then pass it to later snapshots through `GeometryPlan.set_surface_distance_bands(...)`.
The catalogue name of this example's parent is `SURF__MS__chip/left__substrate__upper_air__0000`; `boundary_segments=None` includes all original exterior and hole edges, while an explicit subset uses `SourceBoundarySegment`.
The example starts from normalized input and adds the same request with `with_surface_distance_bands(...)`. See the [planar distance-band contract](../history/sgb-geometric-bands.qmd) for exact parameters.
:::

### Connect caps, hole walls and exterior walls to the same nodes

Distance bands are more than a display mask: they create real partition surfaces that subsequent CAD and meshing must respect.
If a band adds a node to the upper cap, the sidewall and opposite cap must follow the same incident edge chain, or the volume boundary becomes inconsistent.
SGB therefore retains the mapping from original edges to realized shared chains and propagates nodes to every incident surface.

Wall distances are still classified in the original parent's plane and then mapped to realized facets through the existing construction correspondence; this does not introduce a different three-dimensional distance metric.
Z and film thickness are not rounded again by the XY grid.
This example's plan contains 12 such solution-region wall facets, which enclose three volumes together with their caps.

Complete surfaces are also organized into shared points, curves and ordered loops.
T-junctions and collinear overlapping edges are split into shared atomic curves; when two surfaces use the same edge in opposite directions, they retain directional references rather than creating another approximate edge.
Outer and inner loops bound each surface, and oriented surface references enclose a shell for each volume.

Before CAD construction, planning checks parent–child source relationships, materials and ownership, port adjacency, volume closure and group coverage.
An actual exterior wall can be a geometric parent, while a material interface retains its interface identity; a complete parent replaced by children is not built again as another live surface.
Adding bands thus changes the partition without silently adding material or losing original boundaries.

## Construction and meshing: turn the plan into a native model {#construction-stage}

### Build CAD from shared points and surfaces

Planning has already determined materials, terminals, adjacent volumes and shared surfaces. OCC (Open CASCADE) realizes those relationships as CAD.
The polygon path builds points, lines, curve loops and planes into shells and volumes, with incident volumes sharing one surface rather than separately constructing overlapping lookalikes.
That is why shared topology is established first, instead of asking a final global CAD fragment operation to guess material ownership.

This example passes the same effective input with its bands to the existing builder, which produces XAO geometry, physical groups and adjacency information.
@fig-sgb-native-3d shows the full model's native wireframe and curve endpoints read after reopening that XAO; @fig-sgb-native-bands separately colours the selected parent's distance bands.

::: {#fig-sgb-native-3d .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-native-cad-3d.html" title="Actual XAO: native curves and selected bands in the three-volume model" width="100%" height="720" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Actual XAO: native curves and selected bands in the three-volume model
:::

The three volumes in @fig-sgb-native-3d are the Si substrate, upper vacuum and vacuum beside the substrate.
The plan contains 118 points, 132 curves and 26 live surfaces; these have entered actual CAD construction, rather than remaining only a planning drawing.

### Follow the same surface across native renumbering

@fig-sgb-native-bands shows the native band edges and endpoints of the same left parent as @fig-sgb-bands, with colours corresponding to the same C0/C1/C2 bands.
Rotate this three-dimensional view to see the shared $z=0$ plane. It displays read-back curves and endpoints, without adding invented filled CAD surfaces.
Each band child is associated with a group through a stable name and retains native adjacency to the substrate and upper vacuum.

::: {#fig-sgb-native-bands .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-native-bands-3d.html" title="Actual XAO: native band edges and nodes on the selected left parent" width="100%" height="720" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Actual XAO: native band edges and nodes on the selected left parent
:::

CAD import renumbers integer **tags**, so “surface 19” is not a permanent name across export and import.
For example, the following children become surfaces 7 and 8 in this import, but their full group names still identify the same geometry and adjacent volumes.

::: {.askr-table-compact .askr-table-numeric}
| Stable child-name suffix | Exported surface tag | Imported surface tag | Adjacent volumes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `__DIST_0000_0000` | 19 | 7 | `substrate`, `upper_air` |
| `__DIST_0001_0000` | 27 | 8 | `substrate`, `upper_air` |
:::

Each full name begins with the selected left parent's name, while a native tag is meaningful only within its particular model.
Native surfaces outside the physical groups remain CAD diagnostic data; they do not automatically become additional solver surfaces.

### Meshing respects the geometry already established

The Palace mesh builder reads the XAO, groups and controls in a fresh Gmsh process.
`gmsh_default` uses Gmsh's native sizing behaviour without injecting SCGSim custom size fields. Holes, ports and bands are still real geometric constraints and affect the mesh.
A small cut distance therefore adds more than an integration option: it can also add CAD partitions and conformal-meshing work.

After three-dimensional mesh generation, checks still cover tetrahedra in solution volumes, conformity between port and volume faces, and node contact between ports and conductor boundaries.
Only after these checks does the solver receive `palace.msh` and its group mapping.
The worked example here reaches CAD/XAO and native adjacency; continue with the [Palace tutorial](../course/palace-eigenmode.qmd) for three-dimensional meshing and field solutions.
